title: The palette is the product
subtitle: Part 1 of 3 - the style foundation
instruct: Speak as a calm, experienced software engineer teaching a patient, well-structured lesson. Unhurried and warm, never salesy or excited. Clear articulation, small pauses between ideas.

beats.caption: From an empty folder
beats.narration: We have a design, and we have decided to ship it as a library. What we do not have is a repository. So this is where we start: an empty folder, one command at a time, and nothing on screen that we do not actually run. By the end of this part, a Vite app is standing, the design lives in eight stylesheets, three components have come off the registry, and Storybook shows all of it in both themes. Parts two and three take the same project to a package someone can install.

beats.caption: One look, two applications
beats.narration: Start with the thing we are trying to carry: a site that already has a look. Paper white, a deep blue primary, four type families doing different jobs, one corner radius, and borders instead of shadows. Now we want a component library that looks the same inside somebody else’s application, and that application has its own body rule, its own font loader, its own Tailwind configuration. None of them are ours. The only thing we can ship is the design itself.

beats.caption: Three ways, two traps
beats.narration: There are three ways to put that design in a package, and the first two fail slowly. We could copy the site’s stylesheet into the package. Then there are two copies, and the second one goes stale the first time the site changes a radius. We could ship the components unstyled and ask every consumer to match the site, which is not a library, it is a folder of markup with homework. The third way is the one we build: declare the palette once, in one file, and let everything above it refer to those values by name. The package ships that file.

cards.label: What we build
cards.title: Declare it once
cards.body: One token file. Everything above it refers to it by name. The package ships it.

beats.caption: Six layers, one direction
beats.narration: So before we type anything, here is the whole plan on paper, six layers. At the top, tokens: the values. Below it, the theme: one alias per token, so a value becomes a utility. Then the element rules, the house utilities and the prose styles, all reading those utilities. Then the components, written against that vocabulary. Then a build, which packages what exists without rearranging it. And the tarball, which is what a stranger installs. Every layer may refer to the one above it, and may never redefine it. One direction, all the way down.

beats.caption: An empty folder, a Vite app
beats.narration: First command. One folder, and create-vite fills it with a React and TypeScript app. No framework to argue about, no server we did not ask for, a dev server in one command, and the one thing a library needs from its host: a plain stylesheet pipeline that we control.

scene.title: A Vite app, from an empty folder

beats.caption: Tailwind enters through the app
beats.narration: Tailwind version four is a Vite plugin and one import, so the app gets the plugin in its config and then owns the stylesheet. And that ownership is the whole point: the app imports Tailwind, loads the four typefaces, then imports our package. The library never imports Tailwind itself, because a library that imports the framework has decided how the app is built. Below the imports, the app shell: the family variables the design expects, and a body rule, which the library deliberately leaves to whoever hosts it.

lines: /* The app owns the Tailwind import; the package owns everything under styles/. */
/* The app shell: the library deliberately leaves <body> to the consumer. */

beats.caption: The token file is the contract
beats.narration: Now the values, and this file is the contract. Values live unlayered, so the dark class can override them later; a layered declaration would lose to the utilities generated from the theme. A colour is declared exactly once, here. And dark mode is a class on an ancestor, which the consuming app owns. So: one radius, the surfaces, the primary and its pair, the secondaries and the muted pair, then the semantic two, borders, the input, and the ring.

beats.caption: Dark is the same names, once
beats.narration: And here is the part that makes the whole idea work. The dark block does not declare a second design system. It redeclares the same names with darker values, and it stops there: no selector, no utility, no component knows that it changed. Two palettes, one set of names, and everything above this file inherits the switch without a single conditional.

beats.caption: @theme inline
beats.narration: Theme dot CSS is the only place where a value becomes a class. The dark variant comes first, and then the theme block, where the word that matters is inline. With a plain theme block, Tailwind would read the alias once on root and copy the value; with inline, the reference itself is written into the utility, so the token resolves where it is used, and a dark ancestor wins without this file knowing that dark mode exists. The same block owns the type scale, so a heading size is one number in one place.

form that actually matches every element inside it. The root `color-scheme`
* Type. The `--font-*` variables are set by the consuming app — konopskidev
* sets them with `next/font`, anything else can set them however it likes.
* The fallbacks matter: the site's original `var(--font-lato)` had none, so
* outside a `next/font` app the whole stack was invalid.
* Type scale. Body copy is 1rem (the browser default) and every heading step

* utilities both read these, so a heading size is declared exactly once.

beats.caption: One file, a dependency order
beats.narration: What a consumer imports is one file, globals, and it is deliberately nothing but an import graph in dependency order. The animation library, the vendored variants and the tokens are leaves. Then the theme maps those values onto utilities, and the element rules, the utilities, the prose and the sonner surface consume them. Eight files, one entry point, and the order in it is the only reason the cascade is predictable.

beats.caption: The house vocabulary
beats.narration: One of those files is the vocabulary the components are written in, and the card is the clearest example: one utility, one declaration, the radius, the border and the surface pair. A consumer cannot get the radius wrong because the radius is not theirs to write. The focus treatment is the second: an outline rather than a ring, so it sits outside the box, never shifts layout, and stays visible on every surface the tokens allow.

beats.caption: Three components off the registry
beats.narration: With the vocabulary in place, components are mostly a download. The shadcn command line reads components dot json, which points at the stylesheet we just wrote and the alias we registered, and writes three components into the app. Three, not sixty-three: the rest of the library arrives exactly this way, and the interesting work is never the install, it is what happens to the file afterwards.

beats.caption: Then the files are translated
beats.narration: Look at what the registry wrote: a rounded class per corner, alias imports, ring borders. None of that matches the design, and fixing it by hand for every component is how a library drifts. So it is a script, and the script has one correct answer per rule: every radius becomes the one radius, every ring border becomes a real border, every alias import becomes a relative path. Run it twice and the second run reports nothing to change, which is what makes it safe to run on a pull request.

beats.caption: Storybook is the review surface
beats.narration: Last piece: somewhere to look at this. Storybook compiles the package stylesheet the way a consumer would, Tailwind first and the package second, and the one setting that mattered was the docs extractor. The default one cannot see through class variance authority, so every variant degrades to a string and the controls panel becomes a text box. The TypeScript extractor reads the real union, and now a variant is a select over its actual values, in either theme.

beats.caption: One palette, every surface
beats.narration: Three things, and they are why the rest of the project will go quickly. A colour is declared once, for both themes. A heading is styled once, and a component that needs a different visual step says so without breaking the document outline. And a component pulled from the registry is translated by a script that has one correct answer per rule, so the tenth component costs less than the first.

beats.caption: What comes next
beats.narration: That is the style foundation: a palette in one file, a theme that maps it to utilities, an import graph, and three components wearing the house rules. Next, part two starts from this folder again and makes it a repository: the build, the types, a test and a story for every component. Then part three turns the result into one tarball that a stranger can install.
